prompt: What does a consistency level in Cosmos DB decide?
hint: It is not the C of ACID.

choices.text: Whether a read is ever shown a version older than the newest write
choices.why: Right: it is about which copy a read reaches and what that copy has applied.

choices.text: Whether a write that breaks a constraint is rejected
choices.why: That is the C of ACID, a different idea that shares the word.

choices.text: How many copies of each item Azure keeps
choices.why: The copies exist at every level; the level decides what a read of them is promised.

choices.text: Whether two items are written in one transaction
choices.why: Transactions are a separate feature; the level is about reads of copies.

prompt: Put the five levels in order, strongest first.
hint: Session sits in the middle.

prompt: An order goes created, paid, delivered. A reader in another session is shown delivered, and then paid. Which levels allow that?
hint: Which level forbids seeing writes out of order, and which does not?

choices.text: Consistent prefix and eventual, the two weakest
choices.why: Consistent prefix forbids exactly this: an older value, never a reversal.

choices.text: Eventual only
choices.why: Right: eventual promises nothing about order, so two reads can reach copies that disagree.

choices.text: Session, because the reader is in another session
choices.why: Outside the writer's session, session still gives consistent prefix and reads that never go back.

choices.text: None: Cosmos DB never shows writes out of order
choices.why: At eventual it does, and the section's example is that reversal.

prompt: An account in two regions runs at bounded staleness with the documented minimums. How far behind can a read in the second region be?
hint: The minimums differ with the number of regions.

choices.text: Up to 5 seconds or 10 writes
choices.why: Those are the minimums for one region.

choices.text: Not at all, because bounded staleness reads from the write region
choices.why: Reads are served locally; the bound is what limits their age.

choices.text: Up to 300 seconds or 100,000 writes
choices.why: Right: in several regions the bound is five minutes at the least.

choices.text: Up to about 15 minutes, as at eventual
choices.why: Fifteen minutes is what an outage can lose at the weak levels, not a bound on a read.

prompt: A new Cosmos DB account is created at ___ consistency.
hint: The level with a token.

prompt: What is a read carrying a session token guaranteed?
hint: The token names a point in a partition's log.

choices.text: To be served by the copy in the write region
choices.why: Any copy will do, as long as it has reached the token's point.

choices.text: A copy that has applied the write the token names
choices.why: Right: a copy behind that point refuses with 1002.

choices.text: A lock on the item until the session ends
choices.why: Nothing is locked; the token is a header and nothing more.

choices.text: Strong consistency for that one read, at twice the request units
choices.why: It is a session read, served by one copy, at the session price.

prompt: In `session.py`, why did the app's read of its own order go out with `no token`?
hint: Look at the line just before it.

choices.text: Session consistency sends tokens with writes, not reads
choices.why: It is the reads that carry them; the writes hand them out.

choices.text: The client was created at the account's eventual default
choices.why: It was created with `consistency_level="Session"`.

choices.text: The emulator omits the header the library files tokens under
choices.why: Right: no `x-ms-alt-content-path`, so the library stored nothing. On Azure it would have sent `0:0#2`.

choices.text: A token is attached only after the first read of a partition
choices.why: There is no such rule; the write's answer is where the token comes from.

prompt: A read answers 404 with sub-status 1002. What happened?
hint: Not found, or not yet?

choices.text: The item was deleted after the token was issued
choices.why: A deleted item is a plain 404, with no 1002.

choices.text: The partition key in the request was wrong
choices.why: That is also a plain 404: no item under that key.

choices.text: The session expired after its time limit
choices.why: A session has no time limit; it is a string the client holds.

choices.text: The copy had not applied the write the token names
choices.why: Right: *the read session is not available*, and the library retries it.

prompt: One web server takes the payment and a different one serves the next page. How does the second keep the customer's session?
hint: What is a session, physically?

choices.text: The token goes to the browser with the answer and comes back on the next read
choices.why: Right: the token is a string, and it crosses processes however strings do.

choices.text: Both create their clients at session consistency, which is enough
choices.why: Each client has its own tokens; the second never saw the first's write.

choices.text: The second asks for strong on that one read
choices.why: A request can only ask for less than the account's level, which is session.

choices.text: Cosmos DB recognises the customer by the partition key
choices.why: The partition key says where the item is, not whose session it is.

prompt: The product page does 3,000 point reads a second of 1 KB items. About how many request units a second does it need at strong?
hint: One unit per read at session, and the top two levels double it.

prompt: How do the request units of a write at strong compare with the same write at eventual?
hint: Every write is committed the same way.

choices.text: They are the same
choices.why: Right: every write goes to a majority of the copies at every level; only reads differ.

choices.text: About twice, as for reads
choices.why: Reads double because two copies answer them; writes are committed the same way at every level.

choices.text: Half, because eventual writes to fewer copies
choices.why: Eventual changes how reads are served, not how many copies a write reaches.

choices.text: Twice in one region, and four times across two
choices.why: Regions change the waiting at strong, not the units.

prompt: Two customers try to buy the last bunch of coriander in the same second. What stops both purchases succeeding?
hint: Both could read 1 at any level.

choices.text: Setting the account to strong consistency
choices.why: Both read 1 at strong, both write 0: strong makes the read current, not the subtraction safe.

choices.text: A write made conditional on the stock item's ETag
choices.why: Right: the second write finds a different ETag and is refused, at any level.

choices.text: Reading the stock at bounded staleness with K set to 1
choices.why: The minimum K is 10, and no bound on a read protects a write.

choices.text: Putting both customers' requests in one session
choices.why: A session orders reads and writes for whoever holds it; it does not serialise two writers.

prompt: Which are true of an account that takes writes in several regions? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three of the four were said in the section.

choices.text: Strong consistency is not offered
choices.why: Right: two writers would have to wait for each other on every write.

choices.text: Two regions change one item, and a policy keeps one version
choices.why: Right: that is a conflict, and resolving it is part of the design.

choices.text: By default the version with the later timestamp is kept
choices.why: Right: last writer wins, unless you choose otherwise.

choices.text: A write at session waits for the farthest region
choices.why: That wait belongs to strong; session commits locally and replicates afterwards.

prompt: An account has one write region and runs at strong. How many acknowledged writes can the loss of that region lose?
hint: Strong waits for the other regions before it acknowledges.

prompt: An account's default is session. Which request will it serve?
hint: A request can only ask for less.

choices.text: A read asking for strong
choices.why: Stronger than the account's level is the one thing a request cannot ask for.

choices.text: A read asking for eventual
choices.why: Right: weaker than the default is allowed.

choices.text: A write asking for eventual, to spend fewer units
choices.why: Writes ignore the setting, and cost the same at every level anyway.

choices.text: A read asking for bounded staleness on a slow page
choices.why: Bounded staleness is stronger than session.

prompt: `overriding.py` read at `Strong` and at `Linearizable`, and the emulator served both for one request unit. What does that tell you about Azure?
hint: What did the emulator check?

choices.text: That Azure accepts `Linearizable` as another name for strong
choices.why: It is not one of Cosmos DB's five levels.

choices.text: That Azure serves a strong read against an eventual account
choices.why: The documentation says a request may only weaken the level.

choices.text: Nothing: the emulator checked neither
choices.why: Right: it accepts any level and charges one unit for everything.

choices.text: That a strong read costs one request unit on Azure too
choices.why: About twice a session read; the one is a placeholder.

prompt: With version 4.17.1 of the Python library, a program reads the catalogue at eventual and orders at session. How is it built?
hint: Where does `read_item` take a level from?

choices.text: One client, passing `consistency_level` to each `read_item`
choices.why: `read_item` lists no such argument; the level belongs to the client.

choices.text: Two clients, one per level, kept for the program's whole life
choices.why: Right: the level is set on the client, and a client is expensive to create.

choices.text: A new client for each request, at the level it needs
choices.why: Correct levels, at the price of creating a client every time.

choices.text: Change the account's default before each kind of read
choices.why: The default is an account setting for everybody, not a switch per read.

prompt: `terraform validate` passed strong consistency with writes in two regions. What happens to that file next?
hint: Whose rule is it?

choices.text: Azure refuses it when `apply` asks for the account
choices.why: Right: the rule is Azure's, and lives in no schema the provider checks.

choices.text: The provider quietly lowers it to session
choices.why: Providers do not rewrite a declared level.

choices.text: Nothing: validate passing means the combination is allowed
choices.why: Validate checks the schema and asks Azure nothing.

choices.text: Azure creates it and turns off writes in the second region
choices.why: That would be a silent change of meaning; nothing documented does it.

prompt: Match each setting of `azurerm_cosmosdb_account` to what it decides.
hint: One description fits none of them.

pairs.right: What every read is promised by default
The region that takes the writes
Whether the other regions take writes too

right_distractors: The number of copies inside one region

prompt: A reviewer reads a two-region account declared at bounded staleness with `max_interval_in_seconds = 5`. What should they say?
hint: Validate passed it. Which minimum applies?

choices.text: Nothing, since 5 is inside the provider's range
choices.why: The provider's range is the one-region minimum; it does not know how many regions there are.

choices.text: That several regions need at least 300 seconds
choices.why: Right: the multi-region minimum is 300 seconds and 100,000 writes, and only Azure enforces it.

choices.text: That bounded staleness is not offered in more than one region
choices.why: It is offered; strong is the one refused with several writing regions.

choices.text: That 5 seconds makes the account strong in practice
choices.why: Even five seconds is a window strong does not have, and reads still cost what bounded staleness costs.

prompt: Staff watch a dashboard of today's order count, refreshed every minute. Which level should its client ask for?
hint: Who writes, and what does a second of age cost?

choices.text: Strong, because a dashboard has to be exact
choices.why: It is a minute old by design; strong would double its reads for nothing.

choices.text: Session, so that staff see their own writes
choices.why: The dashboard writes nothing, so read-your-writes buys it nothing.

choices.text: Eventual: a count a few seconds old is harmless
choices.why: Right, and it is a weakening the account allows.

choices.text: Bounded staleness at 60 seconds, to match the refresh
choices.why: That pays twice for every read to guarantee a bound nobody needs.

prompt: Which of these did the emulator do in this lesson that Azure would not? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them Azure does as well.

choices.text: Charge one request unit for a strong read
choices.why: Right: on Azure it is about twice a session read.

choices.text: Serve a strong read on an account whose default is eventual
choices.why: Right: a request may only weaken the level.

choices.text: Report eventual as the level of a new account
choices.why: Right: Azure creates a new account at session.

choices.text: Refuse a read whose token names a write that never happened
choices.why: Azure answers that the same way: 404, sub-status 1002.

prompt: Every write to a container answers with the header `x-ms-___-token`.
hint: It is named after the level that uses it.
